stem: What problem does the Model Context Protocol (MCP) mainly address?

options.text: Training larger models
A standard way for AI applications to discover and call external tools and data sources
Compressing prompts
Replacing REST APIs entirely

explanation: MCP standardises how AI hosts connect to tools and data (servers expose tools, resources and prompts). It complements existing APIs; servers typically wrap them.

stem: How does agent-to-agent (A2A) interoperability differ in emphasis from tool access via MCP?

options.text: A2A is about one agent delegating a task to another autonomous agent, while MCP is about an agent calling tools and data sources
They are identical protocols
A2A replaces the need for authentication
MCP is only for image models

explanation: MCP connects a model-based application to tools and context. A2A-style protocols describe how independent agents discover each other and exchange tasks. They are complementary; details of each specification should be checked at the time of use.

stem: An integration layer exposes enterprise APIs to several AI agents. Which design best limits blast radius when an agent misbehaves?

options.text: Give every agent the same broad service account
Expose narrowly scoped operations through a gateway with per-agent credentials, rate limits and audit logs
Let agents call databases directly
Share one API key in the prompt

explanation: A gateway pattern with least-privilege scopes, per-caller identity, limits and logging contains failures and makes behaviour attributable.

stem: Three internal teams each wrote their own function-calling wrappers around the same order and inventory APIs for different assistants. The wrappers disagree on error handling and authentication, and a change in one API broke two assistants.
constraints: APIs are owned by a separate platform team
Security wants a single audit point

options.text: Wrap the APIs once as a shared tool layer (for example MCP servers or an equivalent internal facade) with consistent schemas, errors and authentication, versioned by the platform team and reused by all assistants.
Let each team keep its wrapper and document the differences.
Merge all assistants into one monolithic assistant.
Switch the APIs to GraphQL without changing the wrappers.

rationales.text: One shared, versioned facade removes duplicated effort and a class of breakage.
Documentation alone keeps divergent wrappers consistent.
A single layer gives security one place to enforce policy and audit.
Changing API style fixes duplicated wrappers.

explanation: The repeating problem is duplicated, divergent integration glue. A shared tool facade owned by the API team gives consistency, versioning and a single enforcement and audit point. Merging assistants does not address ownership or reuse.
model_answer: Create one tool layer over the APIs with stable schemas and error contracts, centralised authentication and logging, versioning and deprecation rules, and migrate assistants to it.

rubric.criterion: Proposes a shared, owned integration layer

stem: A retailer wants an AI agent that can check order status, create a return and notify the customer. Order data is in a core ERP, returns in a separate service, notifications in a messaging platform. Each system has its own authentication.
constraints: Agent actions must be traceable to a customer session
Systems are owned by different teams

options.text: Expose each capability as a narrow, authenticated operation behind an integration layer, propagate the customer session identity, use idempotency for the return, and log every call with the session and agent identity.
Give the agent one administrator credential for all three systems for simplicity.
Let the model construct SQL for each system.
Copy all data into a vector store and let the agent answer from it.

rationales.text: Narrow operations limit what a misbehaving agent can do.
A single administrator credential is acceptable if the agent is internal.
Idempotency protects against duplicate returns when calls are retried.
Copying data into a vector store gives consistent real-time order status and write ability.

explanation: Capabilities should be narrow, authenticated and attributable. Writes need idempotency and identity propagation. A copied vector store is stale and cannot perform actions.
model_answer: Define three scoped operations, authenticate each with least privilege, pass and log the customer session identity, make the return idempotent, and monitor failures and retries.

rubric.criterion: Scoped operations through an integration layer
